Public doesn't mean unprotected 1 Privacy belongs to the person, not the place. Puttaswamy (2017) didn't limit it to the home. 2 Being seen isn't being identified. A face in a crowd becomes a name in a database only through the technology. 3 Aggregation changes things. The US Supreme Court (Carpenter, 2018) required a warrant for records tracking a person's movements, though public. 4 Assembly is a right too. Six safeguards the Court should require 1 A law first: FRT only under a statute with published rules. 2 Not at peaceful protests without a specific threat and written authorisation. 3 Separate CCTV from identification: cameras for safety don't need to run face matching. 4 Delete non-matches within days, and log every search. 5 Accuracy audits and human checks: 25 "matches" already in jail show why. 6 Disclosure and oversight: a privacy impact assessment and an independent reviewer. Adv. Ashwani Kumar 07 / 08

TA K E AWAY A crowd is not a suspect list. Cameras in public places can keep people safe. Turning every face in a protest into a searchable record is a different power, and it needs a law, limits and someone watching the watchers. Adv.
